rv.q: It doesn’t look or sound like any other musical you'll see in London, and there’s something entrancing about this icy injection of nihilism into a remorselessly peppy genre.

Arch, introspective, and also about a guy who sadistically murders homeless people, it’s as singular as anything Goold ever staged here, and a worthy bookend to the greatest London artistic directorship of recent times.
Rupert Goold’s swansong is a wildly entertaining musical take on the notorious novel, but lacks killer instinct
Goold’s direction is sophisticated; he accentuates the aesthetic materialism of the story, establishing this solid sense of unease from the very start.
By turns devastating and quick-witted, scintillating yet unexpectedly moving, the piece raises all sorts of hopes for Goold's embyronic Almeida tenure.
It’s still a hypnotic, bloody good time – one that perhaps says more about the macabre dimensions of modern masculinity than anything else on a UK stage right now.
The ensemble cast delivers strongly throughout and exudes confidence.

cn.t: This slick revival of the cult musical earns strong reviews for its stylish satire of capitalist excess and toxic masculinity, with critics praising Goold's sharp direction and the show's timeless relevance beyond its '80s setting.
